title: NS1643 enhances the activity of T1019PfsX38 and Q1070X hERG channels associated with long QT syndrome type 2.
summary: Type 2 long QT syndrome (LQT2) increases the risk of cardiac arrest and sudden death due to reduced rapid delayed rectifier potassium currents (IKr) in the heart. Caused by loss-of-function genetic variants in the hERG K+ channel, LQT2 might benefit from variant-targeted therapy approaches. T1019PfsX38 and Q1070X are LQT2-causing variants reported in Oman and Saudi Arabia. Although nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) has been proposed to contribute to reduced expression of these truncating variants, it remains unclear whether residual mutant hERG channel function can be pharmacologically enhanced. We used the patch-clamp technique and examined the effects of the hERG potentiator NS1643 on wild-type-, T1019PfsX38- and Q1070X-hERG channels expressed in HEK293 cells. We started by assessing the response of these variants under the influence of a ventricular action potential clamp protocol, then used additional protocols to elucidate the drug's mechanism of action. NS1643 [10 µM] enhanced the repolarization currents in wild-type-, T1019PfsX38- and Q1070X-expressing cells. Its effect was associated with accelerated activation rates and a negative shift in the voltage dependence of activation. In addition, NS1643 suppressed fast deactivation transitions. We conclude that the functions of T1019PfsX38- and Q1070X-hERG channels can be augmented by hERG potentiators if NMD is incomplete, which may facilitate the development of a mechanism-based rescue approach.

title: Cutaneous ultrastructure reveals potential biomarkers of ventricular arrhythmias in inflammatory cardiomyopathy
summary: Inflammatory cardiomyopathy (ICM), resulting from persistent myocardial inflammation, is associated with life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (VA). Recent studies suggested overlap between ICM-associated VA and desmosomal diseases affecting the intercalated discs (ID), which are critical for electromechanical coupling. Genetic variants in desmosomal genes cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies and genodermatoses, supporting a potential link between desmosomal dysfunction and arrhythmic risk. This single-center pilot study explored cutaneous abnormalities in patients with ICM complicated by VA, focusing on desmosomal alterations in skin tissue. Four patients (mean age 56 ± 6 years, 50% male) with cardiac magnetic resonance- and endomyocardial biopsy-proven ICM, documented VA, and available myocardial and cutaneous tissue were retrospectively evaluated. Two patients carried genetic variants (DSP and FLNC), while two had systemic autoimmune diseases. Transmission electron microscopy revealed consistent ultrastructural abnormalities in cardiac biopsies, including widened intercellular cleft width (ICW), a marker associated with arrhythmic risk. Similar abnormalities were observed in cutaneous biopsies, including small, narrow, or clustered desmosomes and dermal-epidermal junction detachments. Patients with greater cutaneous desmosomal coupling variability exhibited more complex VA, lower left ventricular ejection fraction, and a genetic etiology. These findings suggest that cutaneous desmosomal abnormalities may mirror cardiac changes and represent a potential biomarker for arrhythmic risk stratification.

title: Ethical Conflicts in Industry-Sponsored Genetic Testing for Underserved Health Systems
summary: Photo ID 64616115 © Sergunt | Dreamstime.com Abstract Genetic testing is essential for diagnosing and managing many rare diseases. Testing for high-risk alleles can predict disease decades before symptoms arise and treatment may be too late. However, cost, limited specialist availability, and health system capacity make patients’ access to this testing unequal. Industry-sponsored genetic testing (IST), in which commercial entities provide molecular diagnostics to patients free of cost, has been proposed as a means of addressing this diagnostic inequity. Because of ethical concerns, many health systems have been reluctant to adopt IST even when it is available, particularly when sponsors are developing related therapeutics. This article examines the ethical and practical challenges associated with implementing IST in a clinic setting. Using hereditary variant transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) as a case example, we assess when and how IST can expand access without undermining professional integrity, patient trust, or equitable care. We discuss recurrent ethical concerns surrounding IST, including conflicts of interest, data stewardship, fragmentation of medical records, inadequate education, clinician autonomy, and the risk of inappropriate testing in nonspecialist settings. We propose that IST is neither inherently ethical nor unethical, but rather that there are five conditions under which it may be incorporated appropriately into clinical practice. We conclude that adopting IST may offer a pragmatic solution to access issues in rare disease care, but it should not replace services that non-industry-sponsored, well-resourced, multidisciplinary care teams provide under clinical supervision. Sustainable and equitable diagnostic support will require broader structural transformations. Introduction Genetic testing is increasingly able to identify genetic variants that contribute to rare diseases. However, results from these tests can be confusing and challenging for patients to access, which is made more difficult by the well-recognized shortage of genetics specialists across the country.[i] In some regions, patients may be completely unable to receive the diagnostic services they require and deserve, even when testing would otherwise be covered by the health system. Industry-sponsored testing (IST)—sequencing and analysis that a commercial entity, such as a pharmaceutical company, provides without cost to the patient—is widely available and has been proposed as one strategy to address “diagnostic deserts” in underserved health systems.[ii] However, despite the availability of IST and these health systems’ capability to treat affected patients who have been tested, many healthcare providers have not adopted IST even where no public alternative exists. Reasons for this lack of adoption include staffing constraints, legal concerns, scope-of-practice limits, logistical and resource constraints, and ethical questions. Another reason for this lack of adoption may be that providers may attempt to follow institutional mandates by forgoing all gifts from industry. This adherence to policy reflects a legitimate ethical concern, but categorical refusal may limit patients’ access and clinicians’ ability to exercise beneficence in strict pursuit of institutional independence from industry. This leaves patients to self-advocate, pay out of pocket, endure misdiagnosis, or receive no diagnosis at all, potentially leading to worse health outcomes. It can also force clinicians to refer their patients to other health systems, interrupting continuity of care and imposing new barriers. Moreover, patients may choose not to complete a referral due to issues with insurance coverage, logistical requirements, physical burdens of traveling while ill, and diagnostic fatigue, among other reasons.[iii] Systems administrators, genetics specialists, and ethicists struggle to weigh the issues with the potential risks and benefits represented by IST. Very little has been written on the topic,[iv] but some reports suggest IST may increase uptake of clinically indicated testing[v] while other data demonstrate limitations in no-cost testing for improving uptake based on patient population demographics.[vi] Given the paucity of information, we use the case of hereditary variant transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) to explore the ethical concerns of IST partnerships and the conditions under which those concerns may be overcome. Case Example Amyloidosis is a disorder in which amyloid protein accumulates pathologically in the body causing organ dysfunction. This protein accumulation is involved in the pathophysiology of many degenerative disorders.[vii] One form of amyloidosis is caused by transthyretin (TTR) protein, a normal protein predominantly made by the liver that transports thyroid hormone and retinol (vitamin A). ATTR has been associated with heart conditions, such as congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and conduction abnormalities leading to the need for pacemakers. ATTR is also associated with musculoskeletal complaints including bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, trigger finger, biceps tendon rupture, and joint arthritis, often requiring joint replacement at earlier ages. Neurological signs of ATTR include peripheral neuropathy, gait imbalances, and autonomic nervous system dysfunction. Early recognition of these symptoms as part of a systemic syndrome is critical, as treatment of the underlying amyloid protein deposition is required to manage these sequelae but does not reverse all the damage already done. ATTR can be subdivided into wild type (ATTRwt, formerly called senile ATTR), characterized by age-related protein misfolding, and hereditary variant (ATTRv), characterized by disease-causing genetic variants in the TTR gene. Once amyloidosis has been diagnosed, only genetic testing can distinguish ATTRwt from ATTRv. A correct, specific diagnosis between ATTRwt and ATTRv is critical, as ATTRv may have earlier onset and more systemic signs and symptoms. However, interpreting genetic results for this testing is complicated. Over 130 pathogenic variants within the TTR gene are associated with ATTRv, and each variant manifests differently across populations. Moreover, patients who are homozygous for a pathogenic variant may exhibit more severe symptoms at an earlier age. While treatment and prognosis are often dictated by the amount of cardiac and neurologic involvement, early genetic testing remains important as certain treatments may only be indicated for either ATTRv or ATTRwt. Different genetic variants are also associated with differing degrees of phenotypic penetrance: some primarily cause either cardiomyopathy or neuropathy while other genetic variants have mixed phenotypes. If a pathogenic variant is present, cascade genetic testing is recommended for first-degree family members, as there may be up to a 50 percent chance that they will be afflicted. Finally, genotyping may identify relatives at high risk of disease before they develop life-limiting cardiomyopathy and prevent irreversible disease progression. While expert opinion and guidelines recommend genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with ATTR[viii] regardless of patient demographics or severity of disease involvement, there are several reasons why genetic testing may not be performed. Patients affected by ATTR amyloidosis may be followed by a diverse team of clinicians. Currently, they are typically treated by advanced heart failure cardiologists and neurologists and are seen at tertiary academic centers of excellence, but this access and diagnostic bottleneck is improving. As the diagnostic pathway has been simplified and several FDA-approved treatments have become available, patients with amyloidosis are increasingly seen in community hospitals and placed under the care of nonspecialists. Because ATTR is a systemic condition, many other specialists may be involved in their care, including gastroenterologists, nephrologists, and orthopedists. In addition, genetics specialists may encounter the disease when screening for unrelated conditions and incidentally find an ATTR disease-causing variant. Industry-sponsored genetic test kits are available for use in diagnosing ATTRv. One example is the NavigATTR Sponsored Testing Program offered through PreventionGenetics, a program sponsored by AstraZeneca and Ionis Pharmaceuticals.[ix] Historically, these tests have not been widely recommended because of these programs’ relationship with their industry sponsors and concerns that the genetic information provided would be limited. However, IST kits offer an alternative route for diagnosis when this may not otherwise be available to affected patient populations. These IST kits are convenient to use and require only a cheek swab and postal drop-box. Some existing gaps in care stem from concerns about the ethics of industry partnerships rather than practical barriers to testing. title: Clinical characteristics of patients with Fabry disease in the Russian population
summary: Introduction. Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder with multisystem involvement, the clinical manifestations and severity of which differ significantly between males and females. The diversity of early symptoms and target organ damage often leads to delayed diagnosis, while timely diagnosis is essential for early initiation of specific therapy. Aim: To study the clinical features of Fabry disease in males and females in the Russian population over the period from 2015 to 2026 for early diagnosis of the disease. Material and Methods. A retrospective cohort study with a comparative analysis of clinical manifestations of Fabry disease in adult males and females was conducted. The cohort study, covering the period from 2015 to 2026, included 259 adult patients with Fabry disease confirmed by molecular genetic testing (150 males and 109 females; median age 45.5 years). To assess target organ damage, daily albuminuria, serum creatinine levels, 24-hour Holter ECG monitoring, echocardiography, cardiac and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were performed. Clinical manifestations were assessed in the overall cohort and separately in males and females. Results. The majority of patients had typical early manifestations of Fabry disease from childhood or adolescence, including neuropathic pain in the hands and feet (67.6%), angiokeratomas (33.6%), cornea verticillata (58.3%), hypohidrosis (49.4%), and/or gastrointestinal symptoms (19.3%). The target-organ involvement, that is, kidney, heart, and brain disease, was detected in 80.3%, 61.0%, and 48.3% of patients, respectively. Despite the relatively young age of the examined patients, many presented various disease outcomes, such as dailysis-dependent chronic renal failure (20.1%), stroke (18.1%), including recurrent stroke, and/or severe left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) (21.6%) accompanied by arrhythmias and/or chronic heart failure. Mortality during follow-up was 12.7%. Male patients had a more severe clinical course of Fabry disease and developed adverse outcomes at younger age. Conclusion. Fabry disease should be suspected in adults patients with nephropathy or left ventricular hypertrophy of unknown origin and/or stroke at a young age, particularly when these findings are accompanied by typical early manifestations of the disease.

title: An Adaptive Wavelet–Attention Framework with Dependency-Aware Feature Modeling for Robust ECG Arrhythmia Classification
summary: Accurate identification of cardiac arrhythmias from Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is an important element of cardiac care, especially as wearable and portable monitoring devices become more widespread. Despite advances in deep learning, the reliability of automated arrhythmia classification often declines when ECG recordings are affected by baseline drift, motion artifacts, or power-line interference. This work introduces a two-stage framework that combines adaptive ECG denoising with dependency-aware deep feature learning. The first stage, the Adaptive Threshold–Driven Time–Frequency Framework (AT-TFF), converts raw ECG signals into refined time–frequency representations using adaptive wavelet thresholding, retaining diagnostically important waveform structures while removing narrow-band and motion-induced noise. The denoised scalograms are then processed by the proposed Feature Dependency Modeling and Extraction Network (FDMENet), which combines dynamic convolutional feature extraction with a Hierarchical Shifted Dependency Attention Block to capture both local morphological detail and long-range temporal relations. The model was trained and evaluated on two public datasets, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia and PTB-XL, reaching accuracies of 96.8% and 93.5%, respectively, which exceed those of CNN, recurrent, and transformer baselines on Macro-F1, AUROC, and PR-AUC. The results show that combining adaptive signal cleaning with context-driven feature learning improves robustness and diagnostic reliability in both clinical and ambulatory ECG monitoring. Ablation and noise-robustness experiments confirm the contribution of each component.

title: ECG Arrhythmia Classification a Lightweight, Explainable, and Web-Deployable Deep Learning Framework Using Knowledge-Distilled GAN Features and Flask
summary: A Cardiac Arrhythmias remain a leading cause of sudden cardiac events worldwide, and timely automated screening from Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals can materially improve patient outcomes. Recent literature has explored Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based architectures that achieve very high offline classification accuracy, but these designs are typically large, computationally heavy, and unsuitable for direct deployment in low-latency clinical or web-based settings. This work proposes an extension to that line of research: a two-stage pipeline in which a cycle-consistent generative model would be used only during the offline training phase to balance rare arrhythmia classes and to enrich the feature space, while a separate, knowledge-distilled lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) would be trained to reproduce the larger network's decision behavior using soft-label distillation. The distilled classifier is designed to be small enough to run interactively, wrapped inside a Python Flask web application that accepts a single ECG sample, returns the predicted arrhythmia class, and renders a bar chart of class-wise prediction confidence.
